html:
Gregory Palamas was a Byzantine monk and theologian, archbishop of Thessalonica and the leading defender of hesychasm, a form of silent inner prayer practised by the monks of Mount Athos.

Born around 1296 into a noble family of Constantinople, he gave up a career at court to become a monk on Athos. Hesychast monks repeated the Jesus Prayer in time with their breathing and said they could see the uncreated light of God, the light that shone around Christ at the Transfiguration. When the scholar Barlaam of Calabria mocked this, Palamas answered him. God's essence, he argued, cannot be known, but his energies, his actions in the world, can truly be experienced.

The hesychast controversy became tangled with the civil war of 1341 to 1347, and Palamas was jailed for a time. Councils in 1341, 1347 and 1351 backed his teaching. He became archbishop of Thessalonica in 1347, though the city's Zealot rulers at first kept him out. In 1354 he was captured by the Ottoman Turks and held for about a year. He died in 1359 and was declared a saint in 1368.
